design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (Comprehensive Meta-analysis version 2) of quantitative studies of people presenting to general emergency departments, psychiatric emergency services or trauma centres with methamphetamine (or related amphetamine) intoxication or dependence. 23 studies were included (17 from the USA, 7 of them from one centre). Clinical features were summarized narratively, study by study, because the studies measured them inconsistently; only three quantities were pooled: the share of attendees who were methamphetamine-positive (17 studies), sex (11 studies) and age (7 studies) of methamphetamine-positive versus methamphetamine-negative attendees. No protocol registration is reported. Pages are the online-first article pages 1–12 printed on this PDF (print issue pp. 567–578).
can_establish: Which clinical features individual emergency-department, psychiatric-emergency and trauma-centre studies (1988 to 2016 data, mostly US) reported in people presenting after methamphetamine use, with their study-level percentages, and, with strong caveats, how the share of methamphetamine-positive attendees and their sex and age differed between studies.
cannot_establish: Pooled frequencies of any clinical feature (none were computed), case fatality among presentations (no deaths are reported), whether the features are caused by methamphetamine rather than other drugs or the reason for presentation (no comparison group for most features; three included studies counted cocaine or other stimulants), or a meaningful average share of methamphetamine-positive attendees (the pool mixes all emergency visits, psychiatric visits, trauma admissions, patients with rhabdomyolysis or chest pain and street-involved youth, and counts one data set more than once).

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL and Scopus covering 1990–2017, run in April 2017 and updated to December 2017, plus hand searching (one study added) (pp. 2–3). Included studies came from general emergency departments (11 in the prevalence pool), trauma centres (4) and psychiatric emergency services (2); 17 were from the USA (7 from the University of California, Davis, Sacramento; 3 from Hawaii), 4 from Australia, 1 from Taiwan and 1 from Canada (p. 4; p. 7).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: English-language quantitative studies conducted in an emergency department, psychiatric emergency department or trauma centre and focused on methamphetamine and related amphetamines. Excluded: qualitative research, samples under 10, opinion pieces, case series, reports, and studies in non-emergency psychiatric inpatient units (p. 2). Several included studies are nevertheless series in which every patient was methamphetamine-positive (Lan et al., 1998, 44 patients; Turnipseed et al., 2003; Hawley et al., 2013; Table 1, pp. 5–6).
sample.demographics: Pooled attendees in the prevalence studies: 56% male (p. 7). Mean age of methamphetamine-positive attendees 28.4 years against 38.4 years for methamphetamine-negative attendees (7 studies, p. 8); study-level mean ages of methamphetamine-positive patients range from 21 (street-involved youth) to a median of 46 (chest-pain patients) (Table 1).
sample.selection_effects: English-only search ending in 2017 with no grey literature or registries; heavy weighting to one US centre (7 of 23 studies, with overlapping study periods); two sets of linked studies drawn from the same data (Fatovich et al., 2012, a subset of Gray et al., 2007; Cloutier et al., 2013, and Hendrickson et al., 2008 and 2010) (p. 4). Most source studies are chart reviews of selected presentations (trauma admissions, chest pain, rhabdomyolysis, psychiatric visits), so their percentages describe very different denominators.

exposure.measurement: Whatever each study used: urine toxicology screens (positive results likely include other amphetamine-like compounds, p. 4) or self-report and clinical attribution in records. Three included studies counted cocaine or other stimulant use (p. 10). The pooled share of methamphetamine-positive attendees was about four times higher with toxicology (22.8%) than with self-report (5.7%) (p. 8; ratio, editors' calculation).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported in the review; the authors note that the pattern and frequency of use, the time of last use and the type of methamphetamine were rarely recorded (p. 10).
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled: the authors state that poly-drug use was poorly recorded in chart reviews and that toxicology screens stay positive for about 72 hours, so a positive screen cannot be tied to the acute presentation (p. 10).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; time of last use was not assessed, so intoxication cannot be separated from withdrawal in psychotic presentations (p. 10).

comparison.controls: For sex and age only: methamphetamine-negative attendees in the same studies (Figures 3–4, pp. 8–9). For clinical features there is no comparison group, except within individual studies (for example Bunting et al., 2007, against other patients with toxicology-related problems; Pasic et al., 2007, a matched case-control study), whose comparative results the review does not pool.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level; Pasic et al. (2007) used matched samples (Table 1), which makes its sex and age contributions products of the design.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Psychiatric history, other drug use and reason for presentation are not used in any analysis.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not recorded; methamphetamine-negative attendees may have used other drugs.

outcomes.instruments: Study-level presenting problems as recorded in each source (Table 1 column 'Behaviour or presenting problem (%)'); share of methamphetamine-positive attendees; sex; age.
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-study risk of bias assessed with a modified Hoy et al. (2012) prevalence tool of 10 items; all studies but one (Marshall et al., 2012) were rated low risk, with a kappa of 1.00 between two raters described as all authors (pp. 2–3). Per-study ratings are not shown.
outcomes.operationalization: Clinical features are whatever each study recorded; the percentages in Table 1 have no stated denominator and no common case definition (for example agitated delirium, agitation, aggression, violent behaviour).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Three pooled quantities (prevalence, sex, age) with subgroup analyses by measurement method and setting.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening by at least two raters independently (p. 2); data extraction not described as duplicate (all authors contributed, p. 11).

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled share of methamphetamine-positive attendees 11.3% (95% CI 6.3–19.7%; 17 studies; 120,111 attendees); toxicology 22.8% (15.4–32.5%; 8 studies) against self-report 5.7% (2.8–11.2%; 9 studies), Q = 12.42, p < 0.001; by setting, emergency departments 9.3% (11 studies), psychiatric emergency 13.4% (2), trauma 17.9% (4), not significantly different (p. 8; Figure 2). Methamphetamine positivity, men versus women: OR 1.422 (1.236–1.636), 11 studies, I² 50.16, Q 20.66, df 10, p = 0.029; toxicology subgroup interval 1.25–1.83 without a point estimate; by setting, emergency 1.36 (5 studies), psychiatric 2.22 (2), trauma 1.35 (4) (p. 8; Figure 3). Age: methamphetamine-positive attendees younger, pooled OR 2.251 (1.421–3.567), 7 studies; emergency 3.108 (3), psychiatric 2.228 (2), trauma 1.286 (0.745–2.222) (p. 8; Figure 4). No heterogeneity statistic for the prevalence or age pools, no prediction interval, no publication-bias assessment.
analysis.covariates: None; all pooled estimates are unadjusted.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA and MOOSE are cited as reporting guides (p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: Sensitivity analyses restricted to low-risk studies are said to have been run for all meta-analyses (p. 4), but no results are reported. The age analysis is reported as an odds ratio converted from age data without describing the conversion.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Subgroups by setting rest on two to five studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Study by study, people presenting after methamphetamine use had tachycardia in 42% and 85% and hypertension in 6.4% and 69% (two studies), acute coronary syndrome in 9 of 36 methamphetamine-positive chest-pain patients, psychosis in 12% to 80%, agitation in 13% to 48%, aggression in 18% to 50% and suicidal thoughts or behaviour in 6% to 50%, in very different settings and without stated denominators. Nothing about these features was pooled, no comparison group was used for them, and no deaths are reported. The only pooled results are the share of methamphetamine-positive attendees (11.3%, much higher with toxicology than with self-report) and their sex and age.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says presentations were characterised by cardiac complications, psychiatric symptoms and aggression with safety risk to health personnel (p. 1), and the discussion calls methamphetamine intoxication or dependence "a catalyst for aggressive and agitated behaviour" (p. 10); both rest on study-level descriptions without comparison groups. The implications section says nearly half of patients were acutely psychotic and nearly one-quarter depressed (p. 10), figures that match no pooled estimate and, for depression, only one study's 12 of 60. The title promises risk factors, but the only correlates analysed are sex and age among attendees, which describe who tested positive, not who is at risk of presenting. The abstract reports a 'pooled variance' of 57.1% in men and 42.9% in women, a quantity that is not defined. Against this, the critical reflection (p. 10) states plainly that the clinical characteristics could not be pooled and lists the measurement problems.

timeline.event: Narrative review of methamphetamine clinical pharmacology giving second-hand frequencies for non-fatal presentations; among its four sources for them is Gray et al. (2007), also included here, so the two reviews are not independent
Scoping review of methamphetamine use and Australian emergency services (Ross, Adams & Beovich, 2017), cited here as consistent on sex and age; not read
Integrative review (Jones, Woods & Usher, 2018), cited here as finding that methamphetamine accounted for 2.3% or less of emergency presentations; not read
This review: by the authors' account the first meta-analysis characterising emergency presentations with methamphetamine intoxication or dependence

replication.where_it_stands: The only systematic synthesis of emergency presentations seen so far in this encyclopedia, but its clinical content is a study-by-study listing from 23 mostly single-centre US chart reviews up to 2016 data, with no pooled frequencies and no mortality. It can be cited as a pointer to the primary series and for the range of reported frequencies, not for how often any feature occurs in presentations generally.

funding.funder: Not reported (no funding statement in the article).
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors (p. 11).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of Tasmania (School of Health Sciences) and the University of Sydney (Psychiatry; Addiction Medicine) (p. 1). Published in a mental-health nursing journal; the implications section argues for mental-health staff and beds in emergency departments (pp. 10–11). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective multicentre study of consecutive emergency presentations with toxicology-confirmed and quantified methamphetamine exposure (other drugs measured), recording vital signs, temperature, creatine kinase, ECG and troponin, psychiatric features and outcomes including death in a standard way, so that frequencies and case fatality can be given with denominators by setting, and fatal cases compared with non-fatal ones.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people presenting to emergency settings), exposure (methamphetamine intoxication or dependence), comparison (methamphetamine-negative attendees, for demographics) and outcomes (clinical characteristics, prevalence, sex, age) are stated in the aims (p. 2), although the exposure admits 'related amphetamines' and the clinical outcomes are not defined.
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Quantitative studies were included and case series excluded without explanation, and several included studies are series of methamphetamine-positive patients only.

Four databases with subject headings and keywords listed (p. 2), but the English-language restriction is not justified, which AMSTAR 2 requires even for partial yes; no grey literature or registries; the text says reference-list searching added nothing (p. 2) while the flow diagram adds one study from hand, reference-list and forward searches (p. 3).
Source material was reviewed independently by at least two raters (p. 2).
All authors contributed to extraction (p. 11); duplicate or checked extraction is not described.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Of the 100 full texts excluded for not meeting the criteria and the 11 excluded on critical appraisal (Figure 1, p. 3), only four are named with reasons (p. 2).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, period, mode of arrival, exposure measure and setting, presenting problems, prevalence and age, but not the design, the denominators of the percentages or the case definitions.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A published prevalence tool (modified Hoy et al., 2012) covering selection and non-response was applied by two raters (pp. 2–3), but per-study ratings are not shown, and rating 22 of 23 mostly retrospective chart reviews as low risk, with perfect agreement, does not match the measurement problems the authors themselves list (p. 10).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects pooling was used, but the prevalence pool combines non-comparable denominators (all emergency visits, psychiatric visits, trauma admissions, patients with rhabdomyolysis or chest pain, street-involved youth) and counts linked studies from one data set separately (Hendrickson et al., 2008 and 2010; Figure 2), with no heterogeneity statistic reported; the age analysis is expressed as an unexplained odds ratio.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses restricted to low-risk studies are said to have been done (p. 4), but no results are given; with 22 of 23 studies rated low risk they could hardly differ.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The critical reflection lists measurement problems (p. 10), but the abstract and conclusions describe presentations as characterised by cardiac, psychiatric and aggressive features without taking them into account.

Variation in prevalence was explored by measurement method (toxicology against self-report, Q = 12.42) and setting, and the wide variation is acknowledged (p. 8); a close call, because no heterogeneity statistic is given for the main pool.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The authors report no potential conflict of interest (p. 11); no funding statement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Critical items 2, 4, 7, 11, 13 and 15 are not met and item 9 is only partly met, so confidence in the review's pooled results is critically low. For this encyclopedia the decisive point is scope rather than the score: the review pooled no clinical feature and reports no deaths, so it cannot supply frequencies of toxicity features or case fatality. It may be cited for the study-level figures it lists, labelled as such and second-hand, and as a pointer to the primary series; not for the 11.3% pooled share of methamphetamine-positive attendees as a description of emergency departments generally, because that pool mixes incompatible denominators and counts one data set twice.

key_findings.finding: Searches of PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL and Scopus for 1990–2017, run in April 2017 and updated to December 2017; English-language quantitative studies from emergency departments, psychiatric emergency departments or trauma centres; case series, samples under 10, qualitative studies and opinion pieces excluded; selection by at least two raters independently.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data sources and search strategy, 1st paragraph; Methods › Selection criteria, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Pages are the online-first article pages printed on this PDF (1–12); the print issue runs pp. 567–578.

key_findings.finding: 850 records, 706 after removal of duplicates, 573 excluded on title and abstract, 133 assessed for eligibility and 100 excluded, 1 added from hand, reference-list and forward searching, 34 assessed for quality, 11 excluded on critical appraisal, 23 included; only four excluded studies are named with reasons.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search results and outcome, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2); Figure 1 (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias was assessed with a modified Hoy et al. (2012) prevalence tool of 10 items; every study except Marshall et al. (2012) was rated low risk, with a kappa of 1.00 between raters; per-study ratings are not shown.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Risk of bias assessment, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of the 23 studies, 17 are from the USA (7 from the University of California, Davis, Sacramento, and 3 from Hawaii), 4 from Australia, 1 from Taiwan and 1 from Canada. Two sets of linked studies use the same data (Fatovich et al., 2012, is a subset of Gray et al., 2007; Hendrickson et al., 2010, used the same data set as the linked Oregon studies), and one pair is a 20-year repeat at the same emergency department. Positive urine toxicology likely includes other amphetamine-like compounds.

Cardiac features, study by study: 9 (25%) of 36 methamphetamine-positive patients with chest pain had acute coronary syndrome, with mean heart rates of 114 against 98 beats per minute in those without it (Turnipseed et al., 2003); mean systolic pressure 148 mm Hg (95% CI 144–152), diastolic 86 (83–89) and heart rate 116 per minute (97.3–134.7), with 3 episodes of ventricular tachycardia and 15 of cardiac ischaemia and no denominator given (Hawley et al., 2013); tachycardia in 42% and hypertension in 6.4% (Fatovich et al., 2012) against 85% and 69% (Lan et al., 1998).
key_findings.locator: Results › Systematic review: Clinical characteristics associated with methamphetamine presentations › Cardiac complications, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Table 1 (p. 6) lists Turnipseed et al. (2003) with 171 subjects, all methamphetamine-positive, against 36 in the text.

key_findings.finding: Behavioural and psychiatric features: police attended 57% of presentations in Pasic et al. (2007) and 12% in Richards et al. (1999a); aggression towards others in 50% (Szuster, 1990); agitation and anxiety in 48% (Toles et al., 2006); of 60 methamphetamine-related presentations to a psychiatric emergency service, 48 (80%) were acutely psychotic and 12 depressed (Pasic et al., 2007); auditory hallucinations in 9 (64%), paranoid thoughts in 12 (86%), suicidal ideation in 4 (29%) and attempted suicide in 1 (7%) (Szuster, 1990).
key_findings.locator: Results › Systematic review › Behavioural and psychiatric problems, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: 12 of 60 is printed as 23% (it is 20%); Szuster's percentages imply 14 people, while Table 1 lists 32 methamphetamine-positive presentations.

key_findings.finding: Presenting problems listed per study without stated denominators: bizarre behaviour 20%, aggression 18%, violence 3% (Bunting et al., 2007); suicidal 25%, psychotic 12%, anxiety 10%, depression 8% (Cloutier et al., 2013); agitated delirium 20%, psychosis 12%, assault 8%, suicidal thoughts 6% (Gray et al., 2007, amphetamine-related presentations, Perth); life-threatening complication 9%, ECG abnormalities 6%, chest pain 2% (Hawley et al., 2013); suicide attempts 50% among 44 patients admitted for methamphetamine intoxication (Lan et al., 1998); psychosis 80%, suicidal 40%, agitation 13%, hypertension or tachycardia 42% (Pasic et al., 2007); aggression 50%, paranoia 86%, suicidal 29% (Szuster, 1990); agitation 48%, suicidal 47%, homicidal 10% (Toles et al., 2006).

Trauma presentations: motor vehicle accidents were the most common trauma presentation in four studies; London et al. (2009) report motor vehicle accidents in 49%, assaults in 22% and gunshot wounds in 8.6% of presentations, and Tominaga et al. (2004) 36%, 17.9% and 3.6%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Systematic review › Trauma presentations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Pooled share of methamphetamine-positive attendees across 17 studies (120,111 attendees): 11.3% (95% CI 6.3–19.7%); 22.8% (15.4–32.5%) in 8 studies using toxicology against 5.7% (2.8–11.2%) in 9 using self-report (Q = 12.42, p < 0.001); emergency departments 9.3% (11 studies), psychiatric emergency 13.4% (2), trauma 17.9% (4), not significantly different. Study denominators range from all emergency visits (461 of 32,617) to patients with rhabdomyolysis (166 of 387), patients with chest pain (318 of 875) and street-involved youth (30 of 133); both Hendrickson et al. (2008) and (2010) are pooled.
key_findings.locator: Results › Meta-analysis: Prevalence and demographics associated with methamphetamine presentations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 2 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Sex: methamphetamine positivity in men against women, OR 1.422 (95% CI 1.236–1.636), 11 studies with 23,434 men (as printed) and 21,365 women, I² 50.16, Q 20.66, df 10, p = 0.029; toxicology subgroup interval 1.25–1.83 (no point estimate printed); emergency 1.36 (5 studies), psychiatric 2.22 (2), trauma 1.35 (4).
key_findings.locator: Results › Meta-analysis: Prevalence and demographics…, 3rd paragraph; Figure 3

key_findings.finding: Age: 7 studies with 1,597 methamphetamine-positive and 40,545 methamphetamine-negative attendees; mean age 28.4 against 38.4 years; pooled OR 2.251 (95% CI 1.421–3.567), higher values meaning younger methamphetamine-positive attendees; emergency 3.108 (3 studies), psychiatric 2.228 (2), trauma 1.286 (0.745–2.222; 2 studies, p = 0.367).
key_findings.locator: Results › Meta-analysis: Prevalence and demographics…, 4th paragraph (p. 8); Figure 4 (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the studies had no consistent measures of clinical characteristics, which limited the meta-analyses to sex, age and prevalence; that chart reviews identified use, its pattern, the type of methamphetamine and other drug use poorly; that three included studies counted cocaine or other stimulant use; that toxicology screens stay positive for 72 hours, so a positive screen cannot be tied to the acute presentation; and that time of last use was not recorded, so intoxication cannot be separated from withdrawal.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Critical reflection of the literature, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: No study row and no part of the results reports deaths or case fatality among presentations; mortality appears only in the introduction, cited from other sources.
key_findings.note: Editors' observation from reading the whole text.

reporting_issues.issue: Turnipseed et al. (2003) has 36 methamphetamine-positive patients in the text (p. 4) and 171 subjects, all methamphetamine-positive, in Table 1 (p. 6).
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator of the 25% acute coronary syndrome figure is uncertain until the primary study is read.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says nine studies used urine or other toxicology (p. 7), while the subgroup analysis has 8 toxicology and 9 self-report studies (p. 8); Table 1 lists Lee et al. (2009) as using both.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which subgroup Lee et al. (2009) entered is unclear, so the 22.8% against 5.7% contrast cannot be reproduced exactly.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints Marshall et al. (2012) as 30/133 (45.3%) and London et al. (2009) as 557/6193 (9.3%); the fractions are 22.6% and 9.0% (editors' calculation), as Figure 2 shows (0.226 and 0.090).
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 1 percentages are not reliable without checking the fraction; Figure 2 appears to carry the values pooled.

reporting_issues.issue: The sex analysis is said to include 23,434 men; the men in Figure 3 sum to 28,434 (editors' calculation), while the women sum to the printed 21,365.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a typing error; it does not change the pooled odds ratio.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and results give a 'pooled variance' of methamphetamine-positive cases of 57.1% in men and 42.9% in women. In Figure 3, men are 2,052 of 2,852 methamphetamine-positive cases (72%, editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The quantity is undefined and cannot be reproduced; it should not be cited as the sex distribution of methamphetamine-positive attendees.

reporting_issues.issue: For the sex analysis, I² 50.16 and p = 0.029 correspond to Q of about 20.06 with 10 degrees of freedom; the printed Q of 20.66 would give I² 51.6% and p 0.024 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; probably a typing error in Q.

reporting_issues.issue: Hendrickson et al. (2010), which the review says used the same data set as the linked Oregon studies (p. 4), is pooled beside Hendrickson et al. (2008) and Cloutier et al. (2013) as separate studies, and their attendees are added into the 120,111 total (Figure 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Overlapping data are counted more than once, which overstates the precision of the pooled share and the number of attendees.

reporting_issues.issue: Pasic et al. (2007): 12 of 60 depressed is printed as 23% (it is 20%); the implications section's 'nearly one-quarter … depressed' appears to rest on this figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: The depression figure in the implications section is overstated and comes from one study.

reporting_issues.issue: Szuster (1990): the percentages for hallucinations (9, 64%), paranoid thoughts (12, 86%), suicidal ideation (4, 29%) and attempted suicide (1, 7%) imply a denominator of 14, while Table 1 lists 32 methamphetamine-positive presentations of 343.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures may describe a subgroup; their denominator cannot be checked without the primary study.

reporting_issues.issue: The search section says no new studies were added after manually reviewing reference lists (p. 2), while the flow diagram and the results add one study from hand, reference-list and forward searches (pp. 2–3).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the search process is not reported consistently.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 17 studies could be used in the meta-analysis, but 18 distinct studies appear across the three forest plots: Pasic et al. (2007), a matched case-control study, enters the sex and age analyses but not the prevalence pool.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; including a matched case-control study in sex and age comparisons mixes a design artefact into those pools.

reporting_issues.issue: Sensitivity analyses restricted to low-risk studies are said to have been completed for all meta-analyses (p. 4), but no result is reported anywhere.
reporting_issues.consequence: Selective reporting cannot be excluded; with 22 of 23 studies rated low risk the analyses could hardly differ.

reporting_issues.issue: Horyniak et al. (2014), whose title (reference list) concerns ecstasy and related drug presentations, is pooled as amphetamine-related presentations (255 of 1,347; Table 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: The exposure in at least one pooled study is broader than methamphetamine.
